title: Adjacency List
body:
The other way to store a [[Graph]]: an [[Array]] indexed by vertex, where each entry is a
[[Linked List]] (or a `List`, or a set) of that vertex's neighbours. You store the edges
that exist and nothing else, which is why it is the default representation for real graphs.

```
A -> B, C           A --- B
B -> A, C           |   /
C -> A, B, D        C --- D
D -> C
```

An undirected edge appears in both lists. A [[Directed Graph]] stores it once, in the source
vertex's list. For a [[Weighted Graph]] each entry becomes a (neighbour, weight) pair.

## Cost

| | |
|---|---|
| Space | $O(V + E)$ |
| "Is there an edge from $u$ to $v$?" | $O(\deg u)$, you scan $u$'s list |
| List all neighbours of $u$ | $O(\deg u)$, which is optimal |
| Add an edge | $O(1)$, prepend |

The trade against an [[Adjacency Matrix]] is exactly reversed: the list wins on space and on
"who are my neighbours", the matrix wins on "are these two adjacent". Traversals such as
breadth-first and depth-first search only ever ask the first question, so they run in
$O(V + E)$ on a list and $O(V^2)$ on a matrix, and that is usually the deciding argument.
